diff_hunk:
@@ -29,7 +29,17 @@
 			<return type="PackedByteArray" />
 			<param index="0" name="from" type="Array" />
 			<description>
-				Constructs a new [PackedByteArray]. Optionally, you can pass in a generic [Array] that will be converted.
+				Constructs a new [PackedByteArray] from a generic [Array].
+				Boolean [code]false[/code] and [code]true[/code] are converted to 0 and 1 respectively.
+				Integers from the generic Array outside the [code]0-255[/code] range will overflow and roll over. For example, [code]-1[/code] becomes [code]255[/code], [code]256[/code] becomes [code]0[/code], and [code]300[/code] becomes [code]44[/code].
body:
Expressing ranges this way is _very_ annoying to read in my honest opinion. The range itself was already stated in the class description, too.
```suggestion
				Integers from the generic array outside the byte range will overflow and roll over. For example, [code]-1[/code] becomes [code]255[/code], [code]256[/code] becomes [code]0[/code], and [code]300[/code] becomes [code]44[/code].
```

But also, it could be argued that the examples are:
- Hard to parse when listing them this way. Harder than it would be to just read "overflow and roll over".
- Giving the impression that the concept is more complicated than it actually is in practice.
- An overcorrection, because given the nature of PackedByteArray, it can be feasibly assumed that most users of this constructor know what an "overflow" is.
- Exceedingly redundant, as the examples below provided in this PR already show this behavior.
```suggestion
				Integers from the generic array outside the byte range will overflow and roll over.
```

diff_hunk:
@@ -4,7 +4,7 @@
 		A packed array of bytes.
 	</brief_description>
 	<description>
-		An array specifically designed to hold bytes. Packs data tightly, so it saves memory for large array sizes.
+		An array specifically designed to hold bytes (integer values between [code]0[/code] and [code]255[/code] inclusive). Packs data tightly, so it saves memory for large array sizes.
body:
I won't really nag about it too much because we've done this for a while, but you can count the ranges in the engine that are "exclusive" with two hands (even then some are only partially exclusive).
There's a lot more "inclusive" to the point where that can be inferred if not specified.

Not sure why "integer value" and not just "integer"

```suggestion
		An array specifically designed to hold bytes, which are integers between [code]0[/code] and [code]255[/code] (inclusive). Packs data tightly, so it saves memory for large array sizes.
```
or
```suggestion
		An array specifically designed to hold bytes (integers between [code]0[/code] and [code]255[/code]). Packs data tightly, so it saves memory for large array sizes.
```

I would refrain from calling them "integers" as they're not "integers" in the way Godot exposes them as. But I guess it returns its values as integers and PackedInt32Array exists, so that argument is moot.
